# 2 Kings Chapter 5 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 226r–227r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_005_page_001.jpg, 2KI_005_page_002.jpg, 2KI_005_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Naaman, commander of the Aramean army, was a great man — highly respected by his king, because through him the LORD had given Aram its victories. He was a powerful warrior. But he had leprosy.

**2** On one of their raids into Israel, the Arameans had captured a young girl, and she now served Naaman's wife.

**3** She said to her mistress, "If only my master would go see the prophet in Samaria — he could cure him of his leprosy."

**4** Naaman went to his king and told him what the Israelite girl had said.

**5** "Go," the king of Aram said, "and I'll send a letter to the king of Israel." So Naaman set out, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten sets of clothing.

**6** The letter he brought to the king of Israel read: "With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you so that you may cure him of his leprosy."

**7** When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his robes in alarm. "Am I God?" he said. "Can I kill and bring back to life? Why is this man sending someone to me to be cured of leprosy? He's clearly picking a fight with me!"

**8** When Elisha the man of God heard that the king had torn his robes, he sent him a message: "Why have you torn your robes? Send the man to me, and he will learn that there is a prophet in Israel."

**9** So Naaman arrived at Elisha's door with his horses and chariots — a full military entourage.

**10** Elisha didn't even come out. He sent a messenger to say, "Go wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your skin will be restored and you will be clean."

**11** Naaman stormed off in a fury. "I expected him to come out personally," he said, "stand before me, call on the name of the LORD his God, wave his hand over the diseased spot, and heal the leprosy!

**12** Aren't the rivers of Damascus — the Abanah and the Pharpar — better than any river in Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean?" He turned and left in a rage.

**13** But his servants approached him and said, "Sir, if the prophet had told you to do something extraordinary, wouldn't you have done it? How much more when he simply says, 'Wash and be clean'?"

**14** So he went down to the Jordan and plunged in seven times, just as the man of God had instructed. His skin was restored — smooth as a young boy's — and he was clean.

**15** He went back to the man of God with his entire entourage, stood before him, and declared, "Now I know: there is no God anywhere on earth except in Israel. Please accept a gift from your servant."

**16** But Elisha said, "As surely as the LORD lives, whom I serve, I will not accept anything." Naaman pressed him, but he absolutely refused.

**17** "Then at least," Naaman said, "let me take home two mule-loads of Israelite soil, because from now on I will never again offer sacrifices to any god except the LORD.

**18** But there is one thing I hope the LORD will forgive: when my king goes to worship in the temple of Rimmon and leans on my arm, I have to bow down there too. May the LORD forgive me for this."

**19** "Go in peace," Elisha said. And Naaman left.

**20** But Gehazi, Elisha's servant, thought to himself, "My master let this Aramean off too easily — he didn't accept a thing he brought! As surely as the LORD lives, I'm going to run after him and get something."

**21** Gehazi chased after Naaman. When Naaman saw him running, he jumped down from his chariot to meet him. "Is everything all right?" he asked.

**22** "Everything's fine," Gehazi said. "My master sent me to tell you: 'Two young men from the prophets' guild have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.'"

**23** "By all means, take two talents!" Naaman said. He insisted, tied up two talents of silver in two bags along with two sets of clothing, and had two of his servants carry them ahead of Gehazi.

**24** When Gehazi reached the hill, he took everything from the servants, stashed it inside the house, and sent the men on their way.

**25** Then he went in and stood before his master. "Where have you been, Gehazi?" Elisha asked. "Nowhere, sir," Gehazi replied.

**26** But Elisha said, "Wasn't my spirit right there when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to be collecting silver and clothing — and olive groves and vineyards, flocks and herds, servants and maids?

**27** Naaman's leprosy will now cling to you and your descendants forever." When Gehazi left Elisha's presence, his skin was white as snow with leprosy.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "the LORD had given Aram its victories":** Right from the opening sentence, the narrator drops a theological bombshell. Israel's God gives victories to Israel's enemy. Through a leper. The story demolishes every assumption about how God works, for whom, and through whom.

**Verse 3 — The slave girl:** The entire chain of events — a foreign general's healing, a confession of faith in Israel's God — begins with the quiet suggestion of an enslaved child. She is nameless, powerless, and the catalyst for everything.

**Verse 12 — Naaman's rage:** His anger isn't irrational — it's the outrage of a dignified man who expected a dignified ceremony and got told to go jump in a muddy river. The Jordan is small and unimpressive compared to the great rivers of Damascus. The lesson: healing comes through humility, not spectacle.

**Verse 18 — The temple of Rimmon:** Naaman's request is one of the most theologically nuanced moments in the Old Testament. He knows YHWH is the only God. But his job requires him to accompany his king into a pagan temple. Elisha's "Go in peace" — not "yes," not "no" — leaves space for conscience to operate in an imperfect world.

**Verse 27 — The reversal:** The chapter is built on reversals: the foreign leper is cleansed; the Israelite servant is struck with leprosy. The outsider finds faith; the insider finds judgment. Grace ignores ethnic boundaries; greed ignores moral ones.

*— PNEUMA*
